t.bumthang@27.5,90.8:
Bumthang is not a single valley but a cluster of four, high in the middle of Bhutan, and it is regarded as the country's spiritual heartland. The main town, Jakar, lies at about 2,600 metres, and is a small place with a big dzong, the Yuedrel Tse, standing on the ridge above the town, as well as one of the country's oldest temples, Jambay Lhakhang, which is said to date from the seventh century. Other temples, such as Kurjey Lhakhang and Tamshing, hold a place in the history of Buddhism in Bhutan, and the valley is full of stories about the saint Guru Rinpoche, who is said to have meditated here.

The scenery is gentler than the west of the country. The valley floors are broad and level, planted with buckwheat, barley and potatoes, and with apple orchards, with forests of blue pine on the slopes and white chortens beside the roads. The food is distinctive: buckwheat pancakes, called khuley, and noodles, as well as Swiss-style cheese and apple products that were introduced in the twentieth century. A local brewery produces a beer named for the red panda, and a distillery makes apple brandy, if you are not riding.

Getting there is a journey. From Trongsa, the road climbs over the Yotong La pass at around 3,400 metres, where the mist, the wind and the prayer flags give a sense of crossing into another land, and then descends into the Chumey valley and on to Jakar. The roads are mountain roads, with sharp bends, drops and few railings, and landslides are common in the monsoon from June to September. Surfaces are variable, with roadworks in many places. The bike must be in good order, the pace steady, and the plan flexible. Foreign riders must travel with an approved operator and guide.

Fuel is available in Jakar, but not far beyond, so fill up before heading further. The nights are cold, even in summer, and in winter the temperature falls below freezing, with snow on the passes. The best times are April and May, when the rhododendrons bloom, and October and November, when the skies are clear. In autumn the harvest brings a festival, the Jambay Lhakhang Drup, with a famous fire dance and masked dances, and the whole valley comes alive.
t.trashigang@27.3,91.6:
Trashigang is as far east as the highway goes in Bhutan, and it feels like it. The town clings to a steep hillside above the Gamri river, with its whitewashed dzong, a fortress-monastery from the seventeenth century, perched on a spur overlooking the valley, and houses stacked on the slopes in terraces. It is the administrative centre of one of the largest districts in the country, and the market on weekends draws people from the surrounding villages, many wearing the distinctive dress of their communities.

Beyond the town lie some of the most remote parts of Bhutan. To the north, the highway to Trashi Yangtse follows a river into forest country, and to the east, the road to Sakteng and the Brokpa people leads to a semi-nomadic yak herding culture with its own language and customs, in an area that was closed to outsiders until fairly recently. Further south, the road drops from the mountains toward the Indian border at Samdrup Jongkhar, descending from cool pine forest to steamy lowlands in a single day.

The ride in from the west is the real adventure. The East-West Highway crosses a series of high passes, from Thrumshing La, over three thousand metres, which marks a frontier between climates and ecosystems, and then plunges through rhododendron and bamboo forests to Mongar and onward. The road is paved but narrow, with hairpins, sheer drops and little in the way of crash barriers, and landslides can block it for hours or days in the monsoon. Fog is common, and the air is thin. Allow far more time than the distance suggests, and do not expect to maintain more than a modest pace.

As elsewhere in Bhutan, foreign visitors, including riders, travel under strict rules, usually with a tour operator, and independent riding is not normally possible, so check current regulations before setting plans.

Trashigang is small, with under a thousand people in the core, so the services are modest. There is a fuel station, a few guesthouses and basic restaurants, and the next places of any size are Mongar to the west and Samdrup Jongkhar far to the south. Fill up before you go on, and carry water and snacks.

Early morning, with mist in the valley and the dzong catching the first light, is the best time to see the town.
t.shillong@25.6,91.9:
Shillong is wet, hilly and surprisingly musical. The capital of Meghalaya, a name that means abode of the clouds, it sits at about 1,500 meters in the Khasi Hills, where the monsoon rolls in from the Bay of Bengal and drops some of the heaviest rain on earth. The town is cool and green, with pine trees, old colonial houses and a lake called Ward's Lake in the middle, and the British, who made it the capital of Assam, called it the Scotland of the East.

The Khasi people, who have lived here for centuries, follow a matrilineal system in which property passes from mother to youngest daughter, an unusual arrangement that shapes the culture. The town has a lively market, Police Bazar, and a taste for rock and gospel music: guitar bands play in cafes and bars, and Shillong is sometimes called the rock capital of India. A local oddity is teer, a betting game based on archery, played daily at a field in town, with results posted on the street. The food is distinct, with pork dishes, sticky rice and jadoh, a rice-and-meat specialty.

Riders come for the surrounding hills. South of Shillong, the road drops to Cherrapunji and Mawsynram, places that vie for the title of the wettest in the world, with dramatic waterfalls, deep gorges and mist. Further on, the villages of the Khasi Hills are famous for their living root bridges, made by training the roots of rubber fig trees across streams, a craft that takes decades. The double-decker bridge at Nongriat is the best known, though it requires a long hike down steps. Elephant Falls, near town, is easy to reach.

The roads are scenic but demanding. Expect potholes, landslides in the rainy season, heavy trucks on the main highway to Guwahati and sudden fog. The best months are October to April, with drier weather, while the monsoon, from June to September, brings spectacular but treacherous conditions. Shillong has fuel, shops and hotels, so it is easy to stock up. Mornings are often clear, with cloud filling the valleys later, and a rain jacket is always sensible.
t.tezpur@26.7,92.8:
Tezpur lies on the north bank of the Brahmaputra in Assam, and it is where a ride to Tawang really starts. The town has about fifty-eight thousand people, a river that is wide enough to look like a sea, and a gentle, slightly sleepy air. Its name means city of blood in Sanskrit legend, from the story of a battle between Krishna and the demon king Banasura, who is said to have ruled here. The ruins of old temples sit at Da Parbatia, and the Agnigarh hill park looks over the river.

For the rider, Tezpur is the last real stop at lowland level. Fill the tank, check the bike, stock up on water and snacks, and sort out your permits before you go, because Arunachal Pradesh requires an Inner Line Permit for Indian visitors and a protected area permit for foreigners, and the checkpoints are serious. From here the road runs north across the plain through tea gardens and rice paddies toward Bhalukpong, where the border to Arunachal lies, and where the foothills of the Himalaya begin.

The heat and humidity here are heavy. Summers are hot, the monsoon is long and violent, and floods are a regular feature of Assam life. Roads are wet and landslides can cut off the mountains, so the best season for the ride is October to April, when the sky is clear and the snow peaks are visible in the north. Early starts help, because the road from Tezpur to the mountains is the easy part of a very long day.

Tezpur is also a good place to eat. Assamese food is gentle and sour: fish cooked in a thin tangy sauce, rice with pulses, greens and a little mustard oil. Tea, of course, is everywhere. The Brahmaputra at dusk is a sight in itself, broad and brown with fishing boats on it and the Himalaya just hinted at on the horizon. Sleep well, because tomorrow the road starts climbing, and it does not stop for a very long time.
t.bomdila@27.3,92.4:
Bomdila is a hill town strung along a ridge in the far west of Arunachal Pradesh, at about 2,400 metres, and it is the traditional overnight stop on the long road to Tawang. The town is home to the Monpa people, who follow Tibetan Buddhism and have lived in these valleys for centuries, and you see it in the prayer flags, the prayer wheels and the monastery that sits above the main bazaar. The hills around are covered in orchards, and apples and kiwis are among the local products, sold at roadside stalls in the right season.

The ride to Bomdila from the plains of Assam is half the story. After crossing the Brahmaputra basin and entering Arunachal at Bhalukpong, the road climbs for hours through subtropical forest, with orchids, ferns and bamboo giving way to rhododendron and pine as you gain height. Landslides are a fact of life here, particularly in the monsoon, and the surface can be broken or temporarily gone in places. Border Roads Organisation crews are constantly at work. Check conditions before you set off, and be ready to stop and wait if the road is blocked.

For travel in Arunachal, an Inner Line Permit is required for Indian visitors and a protected area permit for foreigners, and you should arrange them in advance. Checkpoints along the road inspect papers, so keep copies. In the town itself, the main attractions are the monastery, which looks out over the valley, and the quiet streets where the evening mist comes in from the hills. Small guesthouses and hotels line the main road, and there are simple restaurants serving momos, thukpa and rice dishes. Local rice beer and butter tea are on offer if you are curious.

Bomdila has petrol pumps, which is important because the next reliable supply is not until you reach Tawang beyond the Sela Pass, and the road between is long. Fill up here, and check your tyres and brakes before climbing into the high country. The altitude and cold increase quickly, and night temperatures can be near freezing even outside winter, so bring a warm layer.

The morning view from the ridge, when the cloud clears to show the snow peaks to the north, is the reward for the long climb. If it is clear, enjoy it, because the weather often closes in by midday.
t.sela pass@27.5,92.1:
Sela Pass is the high point on the road to Tawang, at 4,170 metres, and it is the sort of place where the weather is more important than the map. The pass sits on a ridge in the eastern Himalaya in the Indian state of Arunachal Pradesh, between the West Kameng and Tawang districts, and it is the gateway to a country of high lakes, monasteries and army posts. In winter it is snowed under for weeks and the road can be closed, and even in summer it can be hit by snow, fog and sudden hail.

The climb from Bomdila is long and steady, with the road winding up through pine, then rhododendron, then bare alpine grass. Near the top you pass a string of small, cold lakes, including one often called the Paradise Lake, with its water a deep blue-green against the dark stone. Prayer flags flutter at the roadside and the air is thin and bitterly cold. The surface can be broken by frost, and drainage channels fill with meltwater and gravel. The army and the Border Roads Organisation keep it open, and they do an impressive job in difficult conditions.

At the top there is a memorial gate, a few tea stalls selling noodles and hot drinks, and a general feeling of having arrived somewhere that matters. Be careful, because the altitude can cause headaches and nausea. Do not stay long if you feel unwell, and descend if symptoms get worse. Your bike will also feel the lack of oxygen, with carburetted engines losing power and idling roughly.

The pass has a place in the history of the 1962 war between India and China, when Indian troops fought a hard rearguard action in the area, and the story of that campaign is told at memorials further down the road. For the Monpa people, it is a sacred place, and local custom treats the lakes with respect.

Bomdila, on the southern side, and Tawang, beyond, are the nearest options, and the distance in between is a day's ride, so top up in Bomdila. Start early to cross in the clearer part of the day, carry waterproofs, gloves and a flask if you can, and be ready to turn back if the cloud comes down.
t.jaswant garh@27.6,92.0:
Jaswant Garh is a war memorial, but it is also a place with a legend, and the combination makes it one of the most talked-about stops on the road to Tawang. It stands in the high country just beyond the Sela Pass, near the Nuranang river, and commemorates Rifleman Jaswant Singh Rawat of the Garhwal Rifles, who is remembered for his part in the 1962 fighting with Chinese forces in this area. The battle at Nuranang is one of the best-known episodes of that war, and the Indian Army has kept the memory alive here in an unusual way.

The story as told by soldiers and local people is that Jaswant Singh held a post for a long time against advancing troops, helped by two local women, before he was killed. His room is preserved as a shrine, and army staff are said to treat him as if he were still on duty, with a bed made and boots polished each day. Whatever you make of the details, the respect shown by the soldiers is genuine, and many passing convoys pause to salute at the memorial. Visitors are expected to be quiet and respectful, and photography rules should be observed.

The riding in this section is a long descent from the pass through changing landscape. Pine forest gives way to rock and scree and the road follows the valley down, passing small waterfalls fed by snowmelt. The Nuranang waterfall, a short distance away, is one of the best of these, and spray can drench the road in spring. Expect mist, drizzle and rough tarmac, and take care on blind bends where army trucks come uphill in convoy.

You will find tea and snacks at the memorial, usually served free or for a small donation to travellers, a custom of the army posts on these high roads. It is a welcome thing in the cold. Food beyond that is limited until Jang or Tawang.

Bomdila is the last big option on the other side. Carry warm clothing, keep your permits handy, and do not be tempted to ride after dark, as the road is steep and unlit.
t.tawang@27.6,91.9:
Tawang is a town at 3,000 metres in the far west of Arunachal Pradesh, wedged between Bhutan and Tibet, and it is the destination that makes the long journey from Tezpur worthwhile. Above it, on a ridge, stands Tawang Monastery, the largest in India and one of the largest in the world, founded in the seventeenth century by Merak Lama Lodre Gyatso. It belongs to the Gelug school of Tibetan Buddhism, and the sixth Dalai Lama, Tsangyang Gyatso, is said to have been born near here. The Monpa people who live in the district are Buddhist, and the town feels more Tibetan than Indian in its prayer wheels and chanting.

The road to get here crosses the Sela Pass at around 4,170 metres, then drops through Jang and climbs again. It is a serious mountain road, with sections that are narrow and damaged by landslides and snow, and military convoys use it as well. Weather changes fast: bright sun, then fog or sleet within an hour. In winter, snow can close the pass completely, so the practical window is from about April to October. Even then, carry warm layers, and do not rush the altitude.

Fuel is a point to watch. Tawang itself has pumps, but supplies can run short, and the long stretches between Dirang and Tawang do not offer much, so fill whenever you can. The town has hotels and guesthouses, and there is simple food: momos, thukpa and butter tea, plus yak cheese in the local style. At this altitude, evenings are cold even in summer, and you will want a proper jacket.

The quiet at the monastery is memorable. Young monks play in the courtyard, butter lamps flicker, and from the terrace you see snow peaks across the valley. Take time to walk, drink tea and let the altitude settle. The border region is sensitive, so carry ID and permits at all times, and avoid photographing military sites. The ride ends here, but you will want a day to stay.
t.trongsa@27.5,90.5:
Trongsa is where Bhutan keeps its spine. The enormous dzong, sprawling down a ridge above the Mangde river gorge, was founded in the seventeenth century, and it is the ancestral seat of the royal family, whose first kings governed from here before ruling the whole country. Tradition says the crown prince still serves as governor of Trongsa before taking the throne. From the road, the building appears and disappears across the valley for a long time before you actually arrive, because the highway has to wriggle all the way round the hillside to reach it.

That wriggling is the riding. The East-West Highway coming from Paro and Thimphu climbs over the Pele La, a pass of a bit over 3,000 metres, then descends through forest of rhododendron, oak and bamboo, with prayer flags snapping at every bend. The road is narrow, patched, often damp, and shared with trucks, buses and the occasional cow, and landslides are routine in the monsoon. Dawn is the best hour, before the cloud comes up the valley; in winter the air is crisp, in summer it is wet and loud with rain.

The town is small, only a few thousand people, strung along the hillside, but it has a petrol station, simple guesthouses and teahouses where you can get butter tea, momos, or ema datshi, the chilli and cheese stew that is as close as Bhutan comes to a national dish. The Ta Dzong, a watchtower above the town, is now a museum of the monarchy and is well worth an hour if it is open. Jakar, in the Bumthang valley, is about twenty-five kilometres of road away at the next larger spot, and is the usual next stop.

Foreign riders in Bhutan must ride with an approved guide and permits, so the fuel and rest stops will usually be arranged for you, but it is still wise to top up in Trongsa and keep a spare layer in your bag. The mountains here make their own weather, and warm sunshine can turn into cold drizzle in a couple of hours.
t.nyingchi@29.6,94.4:
Nyingchi is the green end of the Sichuan-Tibet Highway, and it comes as a shock after the bare plateau that precedes it. The Tibetan name is Nyingtri, and the town lies at about three thousand metres in the valley of the Niyang river, close to where the great Yarlung Tsangpo bends around the east end of the Himalaya. Here the air is thick and moist, the hillsides are covered in pine, cedar and rhododendron, and the nights smell of damp earth. It is often called the Switzerland of Tibet, a phrase that undersells it.

The highway to get here, the G318, is one of the most famous and demanding roads in the world. It runs from Chengdu to Lhasa across a series of huge ranges and river gorges, crossing passes of over four thousand metres and descending into deep valleys, and the final stage into Nyingchi crosses the Sejila Pass, around 4,700 metres, with views of the peak of Namcha Barwa, which rises to over 7,700 metres and is rarely visible through the cloud. The descent into the valley is a long, wet plunge through cloud forest.

In spring, peach blossoms spread through the valleys of the region, and local festivals celebrate them, while in autumn the forests turn to gold. The area is one of the greenest in Tibet, and it is home to Tibetan, Monpa and Lhoba communities, each with their own traditions. The Yarlung Tsangpo canyon nearby is among the deepest gorges on earth.

Practical matters need care. Foreign travellers need a Tibet Travel Permit and in general have to travel with a licensed guide and an approved vehicle, and the rules for motorbikes are restrictive, so check current regulations with an operator before planning. Fuel is available in Nyingchi, which is a substantial town, but stations along the highway are far apart, and the road is subject to landslides and closures during the rainy season. Allow time for the altitude, and carry rain gear at any time of year.
t.turgen@49.8,91.4:
Far to the north-west of Mongolia, past the salt shores of Uvs Nuur, the country folds into a high rim of mountains where the steppe meets the Siberian forest. Turgen is the name of a river and a mountain massif here, in the Uvs basin, a region that UNESCO treats as one of the great closed drainage basins of Central Asia, with a lake so salty that fish barely live in it and an extraordinary spread of habitats, from desert to tundra, in a short distance.

The riding in this part of Mongolia is real adventure travel. Ulaangom, the provincial capital, is the nearest place of any size, and the way out of it toward the mountains follows tracks of packed earth and gravel that vary with the season. Streams cross the route and may be shallow in the morning and ugly by afternoon, after the glacier melt, and the weather can turn from clear and warm to rain and sleet in an hour. Expect wide open views, big bends in the track, and a feeling that you are sharing the land with horses, yaks and the odd eagle. The short, bright summer from June to August is the only sensible time.

Local life is built on herding. Families live in gers, the round felt tents that are warm in winter and cool in summer, and move between pastures with their sheep, goats and horses. If you are invited in, which is likely if you stop near a ger, accept the bowl of milk tea or fermented mare's milk, called airag, that is offered, take it with the right hand, and drink at least a sip. Snow leopards and ibex live on the high ridges, though they are almost never seen, and the golden eagles that hunt over the valley, sometimes trained by Kazakh falconers further west, are a more usual sight.

Fuel and supplies are the big considerations. Ulaangom has stations, shops and a market, and you should treat it as the last reliable stop. Carry spare fuel, water, tools and food, along with a paper map and a satellite messenger if you can, since phone coverage is patchy. Tell someone your plan, expect nothing, and be generous with the wave and the smile; in the Mongolian countryside, a stranger in trouble will always be helped.
t.lhasa@29.7,91.2:
Lhasa lies at about 3,650 metres in a wide, dry valley beside the Kyichu River, and almost every rider who arrives there from the east is a little dizzy from the altitude, a little sunburnt and more than a little humbled. The G318, known as the Sichuan-Tibet Highway, runs over two thousand kilometres from Chengdu, crossing a series of passes above 4,000 metres, plunging through gorges and following the great bend of the Yarlung Tsangpo before it finally settles on this plateau. Reaching the city is the culmination of one of the world's classic overland roads.

Above the town stands the Potala Palace, a thirteen-storey fortress of white and ochre that was rebuilt in the seventeenth century under the fifth Dalai Lama and served as the winter home of his successors until 1959. In the old quarter, pilgrims walk clockwise around the Jokhang Temple, spinning prayer wheels and prostrating themselves on the flagstones, while butter lamps flicker in dark chapels and the air smells of juniper smoke and yak butter. The Barkhor circuit, the lane around the temple, is full of traders, monks, nomads in sheepskins and tourists.

The road itself is hard on both rider and machine. Altitude saps engine power, the weather can switch from sun to sleet in an hour, and landslides, rockfalls and washouts are common, especially in the rainy months. The best time is generally late April to early June, or September and October, when the skies are clear and the barley is golden. Winter brings ice and cold, which makes the high passes dangerous.

There are important rules to know. Foreign visitors need a Tibet travel permit and must travel with an approved guide and a licensed arrangement, and independent riding is generally not allowed. Check current regulations well in advance, since they change and are enforced firmly, and carry all documents for the checkpoints that appear along the route.

In the city, fuel is easy to find, and so is food, from steaming bowls of momo dumplings to butter tea and a sweet milk tea that most visitors come to love. Take it slow for the first two days, drink plenty of water, and respect the altitude, because acute mountain sickness can strike anyone. The thin air has a startling clarity, though, and the sky is a very deep blue.
